Looking at each chapter carefully, testing only for structural damage per the five criteria, and checking that no finding is a residue of an authorized cut.

**Ch 028 findings:**

The sentence "When Frank Palgrave came one day predicting that Germany would beat France into scraps, Adams thought not" converts a direct dramatic scene (source: Palgrave came, was described as contentious/paradoxical, *said* something, Adams *thought* something) into compressed reported speech. This survives the gate test — the prediction and Adams's reaction are both present. Not a finding.

"The first shock came lightly. Reeve refused the Gold Conspiracy, saying it would bring half-a-dozen libel suits." — This cuts the sentence "as though Nature were playing tricks on her spoiled child" and the framing "He had become used to the idea that he was free of the Quarterlies, and that his writing would be printed of course; but he was stunned by the reason of refusal." The pivot "but he was stunned" is compressed away, yet the sentence still reads as a coherent narrative beat. Not a structural failure.

"Called suddenly away from England, he despatched the article..." — The cause of being called away (the sister's injury telegram) comes *after* this sentence in the draft, while in the source it comes after. In the source the sequence is: Quarterly refuses → called away → sends to Westminster → *then* the telegram. In the draft the order is: Quarterly refuses → Called suddenly away / Westminster Review → *then* the telegram. A reader seeing "Called suddenly away from England" before the sister's telegram has been mentioned will genuinely wonder: called away by what? The telegram establishing *why* he was called away hasn't been introduced yet. However, this is the same sequence as the source — the source also places the Westminster sentence before the telegram paragraph. So this is not a compression artifact; the source has this same order. Not a finding.

**Ch 029 findings:**

"Far back in childhood, Henry Adams could recall his first visit to Harvard College—nine years old, taken by his mother to his aunt at the old President's House." — The aunt is unnamed (authorized cut: Edward Everett and Mrs. Everett are removed). This is a residue of an authorized cut. Not a finding.

"When Adams closed his interview with President Eliot, he asked the Bursar about that drawing-room, for the house had been turned to base uses; the deserted kitchen adjacent was also to let. He took both."

The word "that drawing-room" is a demonstrative reference. In the draft's preceding sentences: "his mother drove him out to visit his aunt at the old President's House" — but no drawing-room has been named. The source says "He remembered the drawing-room, on the left of the hall door, in which Mrs. Everett received them" — this gives the referent. The draft cut this sentence. So "that drawing-room" has no antecedent in the draft.

Gate test: A reader would genuinely be confused — "that drawing-room" implies a specific room just described, but the draft only mentioned "the old President's House" generically. The reader has no way to identify which room is meant. This is a real dangling demonstrative.
